newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel chief says "elements" nearing Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel chief says "elements" nearing Kinshasa.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Tuesday rebels had reached a town only 270 km (170 miles) northeast of the Zairean capital Kinshasa.
"We are in Kasai Oriental. Elements have arrived in Bandundu and Mbandaka," he said without elaborating. Kasai Oriental is the eastern part of Kasai region with Mbuji-Mayi its capital.
Bandundu is a major town 270 km (170 miles) northeast of Kinshasa and Mbandaka is 600 km (375 miles), also northeast.

At a rally in Mbuji-Mayi, stronghold of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, Kabila did not say either town was captured. Such an advance by a large force from eastern Zaire in such a short time appeared highly unlikely.
Mbuji-Mayi, Zaire's diamond capital, fell to the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) last Friday and is 950 km (590 miles) southeast of Kinshasa.
The rebels have seized more than a third of Africa's third largest country since October.
In an attempt to dent support for Tshisekedi, Kabila told 35,000 people at the rally that opposition political parties had allowed ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko to remain in control.

"The real problem with Tshisekedi is that Mobutu is always in the background, manoeuvring to divide the opposition and remain always in control," said Kabila, for whom Kasai is a key test of rebel support.
Tshisekedi, as Zaire's new prime minister, last week offered the rebels six ministries in his government but was rebuffed.
Tshisekedi's Baluba people in Kasai in 1993 heeded his call to boycott new bank notes introduced by Mobutu. Kabila's origins lie with a Baluba subgroup from neighbouring mineral-rich Shaba.
Officials of Miniere de Bakwanga (MIBA) said on Thursday Mbuji-Mayi's diamond mines stopped work for two days during fighting and were partly looted by Zairean troops and civilians.
But the main diamond warehouse at Polygone, a MIBA concession outside Mbuji-Mayi, remained untouched during the looting and was operating as usual on Tuesday, they added.

"Alliance troops came on Saturday evening. They turned back the illegal diggers by shooting in the air. Now the rebels are ensconced in the Miba offices, but they are not yet guarding the mine to stop clandestine diggers," said guard Tomba Kasongo.
The mine is Zaire's biggest diamond producer and foreign revenue earner and produced $74 million of diamonds in 1996, up from $65 million in 1995, said MIBA Director Mfwamba Tchobobo.
Miba lost around 30,000 carats-worth of production during the two-day closure, said Kasango Crispin, chief of the mining department at Polygone which journalists visited on Tuesday.
Kabila received a relatively subdued but noisy welcome at Mbuji-Mayi stadium and tailored his message to supporters of Tshisekedi's Union for Democratic and Social Progress (UPDS).
"The place of the UPDS is not with Mobutu but against Mobutu," he said to applause. "AFDL has a mission to liberate the political class and especially the opposition and for that we need your help."
He reiterated that free elections would follow a one-year transitional period and invited Tshisekedi to stand.
Kabila said South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki had telephoned him in Mbuji-Mayi on Monday over peace talks in South Africa between AFDL officials and Mobutu's representatives.
"Our delegation is there solely to negotiate the departure of Mobutu," Kabila said he told Mbeki without elaborating.
At the rally new local officials were elected by the crowd. Mbonji Mulomba M'safiri, a UPDS joint president in Kasai Oriental, was selected as the governor by a huge majority.
"I am a son of the soil. I support nationalists. Kabila is me and I am Kabila," Mbonji told Reuters after his victory.
